content: 1. Have tuberculosis (TB) drugs been delivered to the facility? Additionally, have there been any stock-outs of TB drugs in the past year? 2. The Above Service Level Costs sheet is designed to assess the accessibility of cost data above the facility level. This sheet is optional. If you choose to collect this information, consult the facility manager or the TB focal person at the facility. 3. What type of supervisory support for TB services do you receive from the district health bureau or authority, and how frequently is this support provided? 4. What type of support for TB services do you receive from the National TB Programme? If no support is provided, list the missing data. 5. Allocations of above-service-level costs are implemented using the Data Entry Tool. Data collection for these costs is conducted separately from facility-level data collection and typically requires an additional week of data collection at the national, district, or regional level. 6. To allocate above-service-level costs to each facility, the data collector completes the Above Service Level sheet, which includes visits related to monitoring, supervision, and drug procurement from national, regional, or district levels. 7. There are various methods to allocate above-service-level costs. The recommended approach is weighting based on the number of staff at each facility. Equal weighting is not recommended. 8. Shared above-service-level costs should be further allocated to TB services based on utilization figures for the facility. These costs include support from the National TB Programme (NTP), other entities, and medication delivery. 9. The Data Collection Tool includes a default list of equipment used for TB care, organized alphabetically. Default categories should be used instead of adding new elements, as the tool has automated links. 10. Equipment price lists should be collected centrally and used for each facility. If the prices paid for equipment are known, adjust for inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI) if necessary and convert to United States dollars (USD) using the exchange rate of the relevant year. 11. The standard and most appropriate value for unit price is the replacement cost. Only equipment used for TB services should be included as capital items. Equipment not used for TB services should not be captured. 12. If equipment is broken but was used in the last year and will be repaired or replaced, it should still be costed. Similarly, equipment purchased but not yet used (e.g., pending training) should also be costed. 13. Derelict equipment that is broken and will not be repaired should not be costed. If it has not been used in a year and is not expected to be used again, it should be excluded. 14. Drug prices for each drug delivered to the health facility are collected. This includes details such as strength, unit of measure, items per unit, order size, order price, unit price in local currency, unit price in USD, and the source/vendor. 15. The Data Collection Tool includes a default list of supplies used for TB care, organized alphabetically. Default categories should be used instead of adding new elements. 16. Supplies price lists may be centrally sourced, but some supplies may have been obtained directly from vendors through the facility. 17. Staff salaries for TB personnel should include every staff member (direct and support) providing TB services within the facility. Gross annual salaries should be provided, including housing and travel allowances, hazard pay, and other incentives. 18. If gross salaries are unavailable, net salaries (post-deductions) can be used, and gross salaries can be estimated using the proportion of income tax and other deductions relevant to the type of employee in the country. 19. For staff working part-time or periodically, gross annual salaries should be adjusted based on the proportion of the year worked. Similarly, average weekly working hours should account for any time the staff member was not working at the facility. 20. Staff time measurement methods (e.g., observation, interview, or timesheets) should be documented. At least one bottom-up and one top-down estimate of staff time per service should be included. 21. Service utilization data is required to estimate unit costs. This includes data on services received by patients in a facility or diagnostic tests processed in a laboratory. 22. Examples of standard utilization data include the total number of people initiating treatment for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) using the long regimen per year, the total number of inpatient bed-days for drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB) treatment per year, or the number of Xpert® MTB/RIF tests performed per year. 23. Service utilization data should be obtained from the head of the facility, laboratory, or radiology departments, clinic heads, or personnel responsible for surveillance or service utilization reports. 24. TB treatment data can be extracted from the TB Register or annual/quarterly reports for TB. 25. Data will be collected for total facility and TB-specific utilization data for the main departments (e.g., outpatient, inpatient, laboratory, and radiology) within the facility, with some disaggregation by clinic or laboratory specialization.
